## Bechdel-Wallace Rating

Bechdel-Wallace scores^[Here is a [video explaining the Bechdel-Wallace test](https://feministfrequency.com/video/the-bechdel-test-for-women-in-movies/).] range from 0 to 3, and are a count of how many of these standards are met by the movie: 

1. It has to have at least two named women in it. 
2. Who talk to each other 
3. About something besides a man. 

A passing score is 3, anything less doesn't pass the test. 

- We'll create `bw_test` to show Pass or Fail.

## Star Genders

`gend_1`, `gend_2` and `gend_3` represent the genders (M or F) played in the movie by each of the first three listed stars on IMDB.

- We'll create a variable called `females` to count the number of female stars (0-3).

## Code to create new variables

```{r}
#| echo: true
movies_cc <- movies_cc |> 
  mutate(bw_test = factor(bw_rating == 3),
         bw_test = fct_recode(bw_test, "Pass" = "TRUE", "Fail" = "FALSE")) |>
  mutate(females = as.numeric(gend_1 == "F") + 
           as.numeric(gend_2 == "F") + as.numeric(gend_3 == "F"))
```

### Checking our cleaning

```{r}
#| echo: true

movies_cc |> select(mov_id, bw_test, bw_rating, females, gend_1, gend_2, gend_3) |>
  head()
```



## Tabulating the New Variables

```{r}
#| echo: true

movies_cc |> tabyl(bw_test, females) |> 
  adorn_totals(where = c("row", "col")) |> 
  adorn_title()
```

Let's put Pass before Fail in the `bw_test` variable when we fit models:

```{r}
#| echo: true

movies_cc <- movies_cc |> mutate(bw_test = fct_relevel(bw_test, "Pass"))
```

## Which shall we choose?

- If our main goal is to create an interpretable model, then we have a different answer than if our main goal is to transform until the data appear as close to a Normal distribution as possible.
- Most of the time, I stick with simpler transformations, that I can back out of easily, like squares, logs, square roots and inverses.

So here, I'll go with `imdb_stars` squared...

```{r}
#| echo: true
movies1 <- movies1 |>
  mutate(stars_sq = imdb_stars^2)
```

## OLS Linear Model (t test)

```{r}
#| echo: true

fit1 <- lm(stars_sq ~ bw_test, data = movies1)
model_parameters(fit1, ci = 0.9)
```

- What does the intercept in `fit1` mean?
- What does the slope of `bw_test` mean in `fit1`?

## OLS Linear Model (t test)

```{r}
#| echo: true

fit1 <- lm(stars_sq ~ bw_test, data = movies1)
model_parameters(fit1, ci = 0.9)
```

::: {.incremental}

Interpretation?

- Movies which failed the Bechdel-Wallace test had a higher average (squared number of IMDB stars) by 2.38 than did movies which passed the B-W test.
:::

## OLS Linear Model (t test)

```{r}
#| echo: true

fit1 <- lm(stars_sq ~ bw_test, data = movies1)
model_parameters(fit1, ci = 0.9, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

Interpretation?

- The data are consistent at the 90% confidence level with (0.07, 4.69) more (squared IMDB stars) on average when `bw_test` is Fail, assuming a random sample of movies, and that our model `fit1` is correct.

## Estimating the Effect with `fit1`

```{r}
#| echo: true

estimate_contrasts(fit1, contrast = "bw_test", ci = 0.90)
```

- Same results as previous slide.
- More useful if we have more than 2 levels of our predictor, naturally.

## Which plots are useful?

If we have at least one quantitative predictor, then we consider all five  diagnostic plots carefully.

- The 5 Plots include: linearity, homogeneity, influential points, as well as posterior predictive check and Normal Q-Q plot of residuals.
- If we have only a categorical predictor (or predictors), then we will focus on 2 plots: the **posterior predictive check** and the **Normal Q-Q plot of residuals**.

## Useful here?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false

plot(check_model(fit1, check = c("linearity", "homogeneity")))
```

## Useful here?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false

plot(check_model(fit1, check = "outliers"))
```

## Performance of the model

```{r}
#| echo: true

model_performance(fit1)
```

- Can we provide some context for the `Sigma` value?

```{r}
#| echo: true

movies1 |> reframe(lovedist(imdb_stars^2), .by = bw_test)
```

## Uncertainty Intervals

When making **predictions**, we can build confidence or prediction intervals using our linear regression model.

- We can do so using `estimate_relation()`...
  - **confidence intervals**: describe the mean across a population of subjects with this predictor value
  - **prediction intervals**: describe the best estimate for a single new subject with this predictor value.
- We can also transform the predictions and intervals back to our original outcome (`imdb_stars`).

## Estimate Relation with `fit1`

```{r}
#| echo: true

estimate_relation(fit1, ci = 0.90)
```

- From `fit1`: Predicted `stars_sq` when `bw_test` is "Pass" = 57.25, with 90% confidence interval (55.73, 58.76).
- Predicted `stars_sq` when `bw_test` is "Fail" = 59.63, with 90% CI (57.88. 61.37).

## Transform and predict `imdb_stars`

1. Refit `fit1` to clarify the outcome transformation to R.

```{r}
#| echo: true

fit1a <- lm((imdb_stars)^2 ~ bw_test, data = movies1)
```

2. Back-transform predictions, with 90% **confidence intervals**.

```{r}
#| echo: true
estimate_relation(fit1a, ci = 0.90, transform = TRUE) ## back-transform
```

## Prediction Plot with CIs

```{r}
#| echo: true

plot(estimate_relation(fit1a, ci = 0.90, transform = TRUE)) +
  labs(title = "Predictions from `fit1a` with 90% Confidence Intervals")
```

## Prediction Intervals

```{r}
#| echo: true

estimate_relation(fit1a, ci = 0.90, transform = TRUE, 
                  predict = "prediction")
```

- What is the difference between these prediction intervals and the 90% confidence intervals we saw 2 slides ago?

## Prediction Plot with PIs

```{r}
#| echo: true

plot(estimate_relation(fit1a, ci = 0.90, 
                       predict = "prediction", transform = TRUE)) +
  labs(title = "Predictions from `fit1a` with 90% Prediction Intervals")
```

## Uncertainty Intervals

We can build uncertainty intervals using our linear model for *new predictor values*, but if the outcome is transformed, we must back-transform manually.

- For **confidence intervals** for the mean across a population of subjects with (new) specified values of the predictors, use `estimate_expectation()`.
- For **prediction intervals** for a single new subject with (new) specified values of the predictors, use `estimate_prediction()`.

---

```{r}
#| echo: true

estimate_expectation(fit1, contrast = "bw_test", ci = 0.90,
                     data = tibble(bw_test = c("Pass", "Fail")))
```

`fit1` predictions (and 90% **confidence intervals**) for average `imdb_stars` across many movies...

`bw_test` | Predicted `imdb_stars` | 90% CI for `imdb_stars`
--------- | ---------------------- | -----------------------
Pass | $\sqrt{57.25}$ = `r round_half_up(sqrt(57.25),2)` | (`r round_half_up(sqrt(55.73),2)`, `r round_half_up(sqrt(58.76),2)`)
Fail | $\sqrt{59.63}$ = `r round_half_up(sqrt(59.63),2)` | (`r round_half_up(sqrt(57.88),2)`, `r round_half_up(sqrt(61.37),2)`)

---

```{r}
#| echo: true

estimate_prediction(fit1, ci = 0.90,
                    data = tibble(bw_test = c("Pass", "Fail")))
```

`fit1` predictions (and 90% **prediction intervals**) for `imdb_stars` for a single new movie...

`bw_test` | Predicted `imdb_stars` | 90% CI for `imdb_stars`
--------- | ---------------------- | -----------------------
Pass | $\sqrt{57.25}$ = `r round_half_up(sqrt(57.25),2)` | (`r round_half_up(sqrt(38.59),2)`, `r round_half_up(sqrt(75.91),2)`)
Fail | $\sqrt{59.63}$ = `r round_half_up(sqrt(59.63),2)` | (`r round_half_up(sqrt(40.95),2)`, `r round_half_up(sqrt(78.31),2)`)

# Analysis 2

## Adjusting for a Covariate

2. Would adjusting for the number of female characters among the first three stars (females) change our thinking about the association in analysis 1?

Analysis 1 conclusion:

- Movies that failed had 2.38 more (90% CI: 0.07, 4.69) "`imdb_stars` squared" than did movies that passed the Bechdel-Wallace test, assuming our sample is randomly drawn from all movies of interest, and that our regression model for `stars_sq` is correct.

## Fit model `fit2`

Let's include both the key predictor (`bw_test`) and the covariate (`females`) in the model for `stars_sq`...

```{r}
#| echo: true
fit2 <- lm(stars_sq ~ bw_test + females, data = movies1)
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

- What does this intercept (60.96) mean?

## Interpreting `fit2` intercept

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

Intercept = 60.96 specifies the predicted `stars_sq` according to the `fit2` model if **both** `bw_testFail` = 0 **and** `females` = 0.

- `bw_testFail` = 1 if `bw_test` = Fail, and 
- `bw_testFail` = 0 if `bw_test` = Pass, so...

## `fit2` Intercept

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

- Model `fit2` predicts that for a movie with 0 females among the three main stars, and a passing `bw_test` result, the `stars_sq` will be 60.96 (so the predicted `imdb_stars` = $\sqrt{60.96}$ = 7.81 stars.)

## Interpret `bw_test` slope

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

- What does the slope of `bw_test` mean here?

## Interpret slope of `bw_test`

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

Suppose we have two movies, each with the **same** number of females in its first three stars, but one movie passed and the other failed the B-W test.

The model `fit2` predicts that the movie which failed will have 0.53 more "`imdb_stars` squared" than the movie which passed, with 90% CI (-2.00, 3.05).

## Interpret `females` slope

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

- What does the slope of `females` mean?

## Interpret slope of `females`

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

Suppose we have two movies, each with the **same** B-W test result, but movie A has one more female in its first three stars than movie B.

- The model `fit2` predicts that movie A will have 2.72 fewer "`imdb_stars` squared" than movie B, with 90% CI (1.12, 4.32) fewer "`imdb_stars` squared".

## `fit1` and `fit2` parameters

What do we learn from this comparison?

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit1, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
model_parameters(fit2, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

- Do the differences in slope for `bw_testFail` make sense?

## Model Performance?

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_performance(fit1)
model_performance(fit2)
```

- `fit2` has better (smaller) AIC, AICc, BIC, RMSE and Sigma
- `fit2` also has better (larger) R-squared and adjusted R-squared

# Analysis 3

## Adjusting for a Covariate

3. Would adjusting for the Rotten Tomatoes Popcornmeter (`rt_audience`) change our thinking about analysis 1?

Analysis 1 conclusion:

- Movies that failed had 2.38 more (90% CI: 0.07, 4.69) "`imdb_stars` squared" than did movies that passed the Bechdel-Wallace test, assuming our sample is randomly drawn from all movies of interest, and that our regression model for `stars_sq` is correct.

## Fit a model (1st try)

Let's include both the key predictor (`bw_test`) and the covariate (`rt_audience`) in the model for `stars_sq`...

```{r}
#| echo: true
fit3x <- lm(stars_sq ~ bw_test + rt_audience, 
            data = movies1)
model_parameters(fit3x, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

- What does this intercept (0.47) mean?
- `rt_audience` had minimum 34 and maximum 99, in our data, on the 0-100 scale.

## Centering the Covariate

In the `movies1` data, the variable `rt_audience` has mean `r round_half_up(mean(movies1$rt_audience),2)`.

- We'll center our covariate (`rt_audience`) by subtracting its mean.
- This will help our intercept term in the model to mean something, since centered(rt_audience) = 0 means the mean value of `rt_audience`.

## Centering `rt_audience`

```{r}
#| echo: true
movies1 <- movies1 |>
  mutate(rt_aud_c = center(rt_audience),
         rt_aud_c2 = rt_audience - mean(rt_audience))

movies1 |> 
  select(mov_id, rt_audience, rt_aud_c, rt_aud_c2, movie) |>
  head(4)
```

## Interpreting `fit3` intercept

```{r}
#| echo: true
fit3 <- lm(stars_sq ~ bw_test + rt_aud_c, data = movies1)
model_parameters(fit3, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

Intercept = 57.64 specifies the predicted `stars_sq` according to the `fit3` model if **both** `bw_test` = "Pass" **and** `rt_audience` is at its mean.

## Interpret `bw_test` slope

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit3, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

Suppose we have two movies, each with the **same** Rotten Tomatoes audience rating, but one movie passed and the other failed the B-W test.

The model `fit3` predicts that the movie which failed will have 1.47 more "`imdb_stars` squared" than the movie which passed, with 90% CI (-0.05, 2.99).

## Interpret `rt_aud_c` slope

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit3, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

Suppose we have two movies, each with the **same** B-W test result, but movie A has a Rotten Tomatoes Audience Score 1 point higher than movie B.

- The model `fit3` predicts that movie A will have 0.69 more "`imdb_stars` squared" than movie B, with 90% CI (0.63, 0.75).

## `fit1` and `fit3` parameters

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_parameters(fit1, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
model_parameters(fit3, ci = 0.90, pretty_names = FALSE)
```

## Model Performance?

```{r}
#| echo: true
model_performance(fit1)
model_performance(fit3)
```

- `fit3` has better (smaller) AIC, AICc, BIC, RMSE and Sigma
- `fit3` also has better (larger) R-squared and adjusted R-squared

## Performance Comparison Plot

```{r}
#| echo: true

plot(compare_performance(fit1, fit3))
```

## `fit3` vs. `fit2`?

```{r}
#| echo: true

plot(compare_performance(fit2, fit3))
```

## Predictions with `fit3`?

```{r}
#| echo: true

fit3a <- lm((imdb_stars^2) ~ bw_test + center(rt_audience),
            data = movies1)
estimate_relation(fit3a, ci = 0.9)
```

## Back-transform predictions?

```{r}
#| echo: true

fit3b <- lm((imdb_stars^2) ~ center(rt_audience) + bw_test,
            data = movies1)
estimate_relation(fit3b, ci = 0.9, transform = TRUE)
```

## `fit3` predictions with CIs

```{r}
#| echo: true

plot(estimate_relation(fit3b, ci = 0.9, transform = TRUE)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "fit3b Predicted imdb_stars with 90% CIs")
```

## `fit3b` predictions with PIs

```{r}
#| echo: true

plot(estimate_relation(fit3b, ci = 0.9, transform = TRUE, 
                       predict = "prediction")) +
  scale_fill_oi() +
  labs(title = "fit3b Predicted imdb_stars with 90% PIs")
```

## Diagnostics for `fit3`?

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(43104)
plot(check_model(fit3, check = c("pp_check", "qq"), detrend = FALSE))
```

## Other `fit3` Diagnostics?

```{r}
#| echo: true
plot(check_model(fit3, check = c("linearity", "homogeneity")))
```

## What movie is the big outlier?

```{r}
#| echo: true

movies1 <- movies1 |>
  mutate(pred3 = fit3$fitted.values, res3 = fit3$resid)
temp <- movies1 |> 
  select(mov_id, rt_aud = rt_audience, bw_test, stars_sq,
         pred3, res3, movie) |> arrange(res3) 
temp |> head(3) ## three most negative residuals
temp |> tail(3) ## three most positive residuals
```

# Could we make other decisions?

## What if we cubed `imdb_stars`?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide

movies1 <- movies1 |> 
  mutate(stars_cubed = imdb_stars^3)

fit4a <- lm(stars_cubed ~ bw_test + rt_aud_c,
           data = movies1)

set.seed(43105)
plot(check_model(fit4a, 
                 check = c("pp_check", "qq"), 
                 detrend = FALSE), 
     colors = c(guards_navy, guards_red))
```

## `imdb_stars` to the 4th power?

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide

movies1 <- movies1 |> 
  mutate(stars_4 = imdb_stars^4)

fit5 <- lm(stars_4 ~ bw_test + rt_aud_c,
           data = movies1)

set.seed(43106)
plot(check_model(fit5, 
                 check = c("pp_check", "qq"), 
                 detrend = FALSE), 
     colors = c(guards_navy, guards_red))
```
